title: Promethazine and Alcohol: Why the Sedation Stacks Up
excerpt: Can you drink on promethazine (Phenergan)? How the two stack sedation and slow breathing, why it's risky for hangover vomiting, the codeine syrup warning, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on promethazine (Phenergan)? How it stacks sedation with alcohol, the codeine syrup danger, hangover nausea risks, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** promethazine (brand name Phenergan) and alcohol should not be mixed. Both slow down your brain and nervous system, and together they add up to far more drowsiness, dizziness, and slowed reaction time than either one alone. At higher doses, or on top of other sedating drugs, the combination can slow your breathing. The prescribing information for promethazine tells people to avoid alcohol while taking it. If you've been prescribed promethazine and want to know whether you can have a drink, the person to ask is your prescriber or pharmacist, because the answer depends on your dose, the form you take, your other medicines, and your health.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink while promethazine is working in your body, and don't take promethazine to "fix" vomiting while you're still drunk. Never mix alcohol with **promethazine with codeine** cough syrup, which contains an opioid. Don't drive after taking promethazine until you know how it affects you, and never after combining it with alcohol. If you take promethazine regularly, ask your prescriber how long to wait after a dose before drinking, or whether you should skip alcohol entirely.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor, prescriber, or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Call 911 or your local emergency number right away if** someone who has mixed promethazine and alcohol (or any sedating medicine and alcohol) is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is confused and can't stay awake, has a seizure, or is vomiting while too drowsy to protect their airway. If someone is drowsy and vomiting, roll them onto their side and stay with them. For questions about a possible overdose that is not an emergency, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## What Promethazine Is and Why It's Prescribed

Promethazine is an older prescription medicine with several jobs. Doctors use it to:

- **Treat and prevent nausea and vomiting**, including after surgery, during stomach bugs, and sometimes in pregnancy.
- **Prevent and treat motion sickness.**
- **Relieve allergy symptoms** such as itching, hives, and a runny nose.
- **Cause sedation** before or after surgery or other procedures, or to help with sleep in certain short-term situations.
- **Calm coughs**, when it's combined with other drugs in prescription cough syrups.

It comes as tablets, oral syrup, rectal suppositories, and an injection. It's also an ingredient in two common prescription cough syrups: **promethazine DM** (with dextromethorphan) and **promethazine with codeine** (with an opioid). Those combinations matter a lot when alcohol is involved, and we cover them in their own section below.

Chemically, promethazine is a **phenothiazine**, a family of drugs that also includes some older antipsychotic medicines. It's usually grouped with first-generation antihistamines, the same broad class as diphenhydramine (Benadryl), but it acts on more systems in the brain than a typical allergy pill. That's why it works so well against nausea, and it's also why it's so sedating.

## How Promethazine and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

The main problem is simple: **both drugs depress the central nervous system** (your brain and spinal cord). When you take two depressants together, their effects stack. The promethazine label describes its sedating action as additive with other central nervous system depressants and names alcohol specifically.

Here's what promethazine does that makes it clash with alcohol:

1. **It blocks histamine H1 receptors in the brain.** Histamine helps keep you awake and alert. Blocking it causes drowsiness. This is the same reason older antihistamines like Benadryl make you sleepy. Our guide to [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) explains why first-generation antihistamines are the ones to watch.
2. **It blocks dopamine receptors.** This is a big part of how it stops nausea, since dopamine signals in the brain's vomiting center help trigger it. Dopamine blockade also adds to sedation and slowed movement.
3. **It has strong anticholinergic effects.** It blocks acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, attention, and many body functions. That causes dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, trouble urinating, and in some people (especially older adults) confusion.
4. **It blocks alpha-adrenergic receptors.** These help keep your blood vessels tight. Blocking them can lower your blood pressure, especially when you stand up quickly.

Alcohol, meanwhile, boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory signal (glutamate). The result is slower thinking, slower reflexes, poorer coordination, and, at high enough levels, slowed breathing.

Put them together and you get the same direction of effect from several angles at once. The practical result is:

- **Much heavier drowsiness.** People can fall asleep suddenly or be very hard to wake.
- **Worse coordination and judgment.** This raises the risk of falls, injuries, and car crashes.
- **Dizziness and fainting.** Alcohol widens blood vessels and promotes fluid loss, and promethazine can lower blood pressure. Add the dehydration that comes from vomiting, and standing up can make you lightheaded or make you pass out.
- **More confusion and memory gaps**, particularly in older adults.
- **Slowed or shallow breathing** at higher doses, when other depressants are involved, or in people with lung or sleep-breathing problems.

### Why breathing is the part to take seriously

Promethazine carries an FDA boxed warning, the strongest warning on a prescription label, against use in **children under 2 years old** because it has caused fatal breathing problems in that age group. The label also advises caution in people with breathing conditions such as COPD or sleep apnea. In healthy adults taking a normal dose, promethazine alone is not usually a breathing danger. But alcohol is also a respiratory depressant, and the two together push in the same direction. The risk climbs further if you've also taken an opioid, a benzodiazepine, a sleep medicine, or a muscle relaxer.

If you have sleep apnea, this is worth knowing on its own: alcohol already relaxes the throat muscles and worsens apnea, as explained in our guide to [alcohol and sleep apnea](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-sleep-apnea). Adding a strong sedative on top makes that worse.

### The vomiting problem

There's a specific danger that comes up because of what promethazine is used for. Someone who has been drinking heavily starts vomiting, and they (or a friend) reach for a leftover promethazine prescription to stop it. That's a risky move for two reasons:

- **Heavy sedation plus vomiting is a choking risk.** If a person is too drowsy to wake up and clear their airway, they can inhale vomit into their lungs. This is one of the ways alcohol poisoning becomes deadly, and a sedating anti-nausea drug can deepen the drowsiness that makes it possible.
- **Vomiting after drinking can be a sign of alcohol poisoning.** Stopping the vomiting with a sedative doesn't fix the underlying problem. It can hide it while the person becomes more sedated.

If someone has been drinking heavily and is vomiting, the right response is to keep them on their side, stay with them, and get emergency help if they show any of the danger signs listed in the box at the top. Don't give them promethazine or any other sedating medicine.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Say

You don't need to rely on anyone's opinion here. The guidance is written into the drug's own labeling.

- **Avoid alcohol.** The FDA-approved prescribing information for promethazine tells patients to avoid alcohol and other central nervous system depressants while taking it, and warns that promethazine may impair the mental and physical abilities needed for driving or operating machinery.
- **Other depressants may need lower doses.** The label notes that when promethazine is given alongside other sedating drugs such as opioids and barbiturates, those doses often need to be reduced or the drugs avoided. That's a decision for the prescriber, not something to work out yourself, but it tells you how seriously the stacking effect is taken in medicine.
- **Older adults.** The American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria, a widely used list of medicines that are often a poor fit for older adults, includes first-generation antihistamines such as promethazine because of their anticholinergic effects, confusion, and fall risk. Alcohol adds to every one of those problems.
- **Children.** Promethazine should not be used in children under 2, and it's used cautiously in older children. This article is about adults.

Pharmacies typically put a "may cause drowsiness; alcohol may intensify this effect" sticker on the bottle. That sticker is there for a reason.

## Promethazine With Codeine: Do Not Combine With Alcohol

This deserves its own section because it's the most dangerous version of this question.

**Promethazine with codeine** is a prescription cough syrup that combines promethazine with codeine, an opioid. Opioids slow breathing directly, and that effect is the main way opioid overdoses kill. Alcohol is also a depressant, and promethazine adds still more sedation. Mixing all three is a well-recognized route to dangerous breathing problems, overdose, and death.

The FDA has added boxed warnings to opioid products, including codeine cough medicines, about the serious risks of combining them with other central nervous system depressants, which includes alcohol. The FDA has also limited prescription opioid cough and cold medicines to adults 18 and older.

The rules here are strict:

- **Do not drink any alcohol while taking promethazine with codeine.**
- **Do not take more than prescribed**, and don't combine it with other sedatives, sleep aids, or anxiety medicines unless your prescriber has specifically said so.
- **Never use it outside of a prescription.** Mixing codeine-promethazine syrup with soda or alcohol is a known form of drug misuse, and it has led to fatal overdoses.
- **Know the emergency signs:** very slow or stopped breathing, blue or gray lips, pinpoint pupils, limpness, gurgling or snoring sounds, and being unable to wake. If you see these, call 911 immediately. If naloxone (Narcan) is available, use it as directed, and stay with the person until help arrives.

**Promethazine DM** is different: it contains dextromethorphan, not an opioid. It's still sedating, and dextromethorphan can add dizziness and confusion, so the same "avoid alcohol" advice applies. Check your bottle so you know which one you have.

## How Long After Promethazine Can You Drink?

There's no single official waiting period that fits everyone, and this is exactly the question to bring to your prescriber or pharmacist. Here's what affects the answer:

- **How long it works.** A single oral dose usually starts working within about 20 minutes, and its effects typically last around 4 to 6 hours, sometimes up to 12. Many people feel drowsy or "hung over" the next morning after a dose taken at night.
- **How long it stays in your body.** Promethazine has a long elimination half-life (the time for your body to clear half the drug), and the drug is still present in your system after the noticeable effects fade. The amount left drops over the following day or so.
- **How often you take it.** If you're taking it every 4 to 6 hours for ongoing nausea, there's no real gap in which alcohol would be safe.
- **What else you take.** Opioids, sleep medicines, anxiety medicines, and other sedatives change the picture completely.
- **Your age, liver health, and lung health.** Older adults and people with liver disease may clear the drug more slowly. People with breathing conditions are more vulnerable to the respiratory effects.

A sensible approach is to treat the whole period you're taking promethazine as an alcohol-free stretch. If you need to take it for a few days for a stomach bug or after surgery, that's usually not a big sacrifice, especially since you're probably not feeling up to drinking anyway. If you take it regularly or as needed for a longer-term condition, ask your prescriber directly how to handle alcohol, and follow their answer.

## Can You Take Promethazine for Hangover Nausea?

This is one of the most common reasons people search for this topic, so it's worth answering head-on.

**Not while alcohol is still in your system.** Hangover vomiting often starts while there's still alcohol in your blood, sometimes a lot of it. Taking a strong sedative at that point stacks the two depressants, and if you're also vomiting, it adds the choking risk we described above.

**Only if it's prescribed to you, and only with your prescriber's okay for that use.** Promethazine is a prescription drug. Using someone else's, or an old prescription for a different reason, means nobody has checked whether it's appropriate for you right now. A pharmacist can tell you whether your prescription is a reasonable choice for nausea after drinking and how long to wait.

**There are gentler first steps.** Most hangover nausea settles on its own with time, small sips of fluid, and bland food. Our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what helps and what to avoid.

**Get medical help if vomiting won't stop.** If you can't keep fluids down for many hours, are vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, have severe belly pain, are very dizzy or confused, or show signs of dehydration (very little urine, a racing heart, fainting), see a doctor or go to urgent care. Repeated vomiting after drinking can also be a sign of alcohol poisoning, which needs emergency care.

## Promethazine vs. Other Anti-Nausea Medicines With Alcohol

People often ask whether a different anti-nausea medicine would be "safer" with alcohol. The honest answer is that none of them are a green light, but they don't all carry the same type of risk.

| Medicine | How sedating? | Main concern with alcohol | Prescription? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Promethazine (Phenergan) | Strongly | Stacked sedation, dizziness, low blood pressure, slowed breathing at higher doses | Yes |
| Ondansetron (Zofran) | Usually not very | Heart rhythm (QT) effects; alcohol can't be "treated" by blocking nausea | Yes |
| Meclizine (Antivert, Bonine) | Moderately | Added drowsiness and dizziness | Some forms OTC |
| Dimenhydrinate (Dramamine) | Strongly | Added drowsiness, confusion | OTC |
| Metoclopramide (Reglan) | Somewhat | Added sedation; can worsen alertness | Yes |

**Ondansetron (Zofran)** works differently. It blocks serotonin signals that trigger vomiting and is usually much less sedating than promethazine. That doesn't make it a free pass with alcohol. It has its own heart rhythm concerns. Our full guide to [Zofran and alcohol](/never-hungover/zofran-and-alcohol) covers it in detail. If drowsiness is a problem for you, ask your prescriber whether a less sedating anti-nausea option makes sense.

**Over-the-counter motion sickness pills** like meclizine and dimenhydrinate are also antihistamines and also stack with alcohol. See [meclizine and alcohol](/never-hungover/meclizine-and-alcohol) and [Dramamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/dramamine-and-alcohol) for details.

The pattern across all of them: the more sedating the medicine, the more it stacks with alcohol.

## Other Medicines That Make the Combination More Dangerous

Promethazine plus alcohol is a two-depressant combination. Each extra sedating drug you add raises the risk. Be especially careful with, and talk to your prescriber about, any of these:

- **Opioids**, including codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone, tramadol, and others. This is the highest-risk combination.
- **Benzodiazepines**, such as alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), and lorazepam (Ativan). See our guide to [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol).
- **Sleep medicines**, such as zolpidem (Ambien) and other prescription or over-the-counter sleep aids. Our [sleep aids and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) guide explains why these add up.
- **Other antihistamines**, including diphenhydramine (Benadryl, many "PM" products), doxylamine (Unisom, NyQuil), and hydroxyzine. Taking two sedating antihistamines at once doubles up on the same effects. Our [hydroxyzine and alcohol](/never-hungover/hydroxyzine-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) guides explain the overlap.
- **Muscle relaxers**, gabapentin, and pregabalin.
- **Some antidepressants and antipsychotics**, which can add sedation or anticholinergic effects.
- **Cannabis**, which also adds drowsiness and slows reaction time.

Check the labels of over-the-counter cold, flu, and sleep products. Many contain a sedating antihistamine, and some liquid cold medicines also contain alcohol.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Talk with your prescriber before using promethazine at all, and ask specifically about alcohol, if you:

- **Are an older adult.** Confusion, falls, and constipation or urinary retention are more likely, and alcohol worsens each one.
- **Have sleep apnea, COPD, asthma, or other breathing problems.**
- **Have a seizure disorder.** Promethazine can lower the seizure threshold, and alcohol and alcohol withdrawal affect seizure risk too.
- **Have liver disease**, which can slow how quickly your body clears the drug.
- **Have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or trouble urinating**, since the anticholinergic effects can worsen these.
- **Have low blood pressure** or a history of fainting.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** Promethazine is sometimes used for nausea in pregnancy under a doctor's care. Alcohol isn't considered safe in pregnancy at any amount.
- **Take any of the sedating medicines listed above.**

## Side Effects to Watch For

Even without alcohol, promethazine can cause side effects you should know about. Alcohol tends to make the common ones worse.

**Common:** drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and feeling groggy the next day.

**Call your prescriber if you notice:** confusion, restlessness or agitation (some people, especially children and older adults, get a paradoxical "wired" reaction), trouble urinating, ringing in the ears, unusual muscle movements (stiffness, twitching, or a stuck gaze), or yellowing of the skin or eyes.

**Get emergency help for:** slow or troubled breathing, fainting, a seizure, a very high fever with stiff muscles and confusion (a rare but serious reaction called neuroleptic malignant syndrome), or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as swelling of the face or throat.

**If you received promethazine by injection** and notice severe pain, swelling, blistering, or color changes at or near the injection site, contact a doctor right away. The injectable form carries a boxed warning about severe tissue injury.

## If You've Already Mixed Them

If you took a normal prescribed dose of promethazine and had a drink or two, the most likely result is that you'll feel much drowsier and dizzier than usual. Here's what to do:

1. **Stop drinking** and don't take another dose of promethazine or any other sedating medicine.
2. **Don't drive**, and don't do anything that needs balance or quick reactions.
3. **Don't be alone if you feel very sleepy.** Ask someone to check on you.
4. **Sit or lie down, and stand up slowly** to avoid fainting.
5. **Sip water** if you can keep it down.
6. **Call your pharmacist, prescriber, or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US)** if you're unsure whether you need care. They can tell you what to watch for based on your dose and how much you drank.
7. **Call 911** if you or someone else shows any of the emergency signs in the box at the top of this page: hard to wake, slow or irregular breathing, blue lips, seizure, or vomiting while too drowsy to protect the airway.

If you also took promethazine with codeine, an opioid, or another sedative along with alcohol, treat it as a potential emergency and get medical advice right away, even if you feel okay at first.

## Practical Tips If You're Prescribed Promethazine

- **Ask your prescriber about alcohol when you get the prescription.** It's a normal question, and the answer may depend on why you're taking it and for how long.
- **Ask your pharmacist to check your full medicine list**, including over-the-counter sleep aids, allergy pills, and cold medicines.
- **Know which product you have.** Plain promethazine, promethazine DM, and promethazine with codeine are very different when it comes to alcohol.
- **Plan around the sedation.** Take it when you can rest, and don't drive until you know how it affects you.
- **Store it safely** and don't share it. Keep it away from children, especially children under 2.
- **Save drinking for after you're done with the course**, once you're feeling well and your prescriber agrees it's fine.

## Where DHM Fits, and Where It Doesn't

Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a plant compound some people take on nights they drink. Research on DHM is promising but still early, mostly from animal and lab studies with limited human data. It is not an anti-nausea medicine, it doesn't reverse sedation, and it does **not** make it safer to combine alcohol with promethazine or any other sedating drug. Some animal research suggests DHM acts on GABA-A receptors, part of the same calming system alcohol affects, and there's little human data on how it interacts with sedating medicines. So don't add it to a night where you've taken promethazine, and if you take any sedating medicine regularly, ask your prescriber or pharmacist before trying it. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what's known.

On nights when you aren't taking any sedating medicine, some people use DHM as one part of a broader approach that matters more: pacing, alternating with water, eating, and stopping earlier. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers those habits. If you want to try DHM, a simple single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and the [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing.

## The Bottom Line

Promethazine is an effective anti-nausea and allergy medicine, but it's also a strong sedative, and alcohol multiplies that sedation. Together they cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and in some situations slowed breathing. The label says to avoid alcohol. Don't use promethazine to stop vomiting while you're still drunk, never mix alcohol with promethazine with codeine, and don't drive after taking either. For anything beyond that, including how long to wait after your last dose, ask your prescriber or pharmacist and follow their advice.

faq.question: Can you drink alcohol while taking promethazine?
faq.answer: It's not recommended. Promethazine and alcohol both depress the central nervous system, so together they cause much more drowsiness, dizziness, and slowed reaction time, and at higher doses or with other sedatives they can slow breathing. The prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol. If you have questions about your specific situation, ask your prescriber or pharmacist.

faq.question: How long after taking promethazine can I drink alcohol?
faq.answer: There's no single official waiting period. A dose usually works for about 4 to 6 hours, sometimes up to 12, and the drug stays in your body longer than that, which is why many people feel groggy the next day. The safest approach is to avoid alcohol for the whole time you're taking promethazine and ask your prescriber or pharmacist how long to wait after your last dose.

faq.question: Can I take promethazine for hangover nausea?
faq.answer: Not while alcohol is still in your system, and only if it's prescribed to you and your prescriber agrees it's appropriate. Combining promethazine with alcohol stacks sedation, and being heavily sedated while vomiting raises the risk of choking. If vomiting after drinking won't stop, or the person is very drowsy or confused, get medical help instead of giving a sedative.

faq.question: Is promethazine with codeine dangerous with alcohol?
faq.answer: Yes. Promethazine with codeine contains an opioid, and opioids, alcohol, and promethazine all slow breathing and brain activity. The FDA requires boxed warnings on opioid medicines about combining them with other central nervous system depressants, including alcohol. Do not drink at all while taking it. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has blue lips.

faq.question: What happens if you mix Phenergan and alcohol?
faq.answer: Most people feel much sleepier and dizzier than usual, with poor coordination and slower thinking. Some feel faint when standing because both can lower blood pressure. At higher doses, with other sedating drugs, or in people with breathing problems, the combination can slow breathing. Stop drinking, don't drive, don't stay alone if very drowsy, and call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or 911 depending on how severe the symptoms are.

faq.question: Is Zofran safer than promethazine with alcohol?
faq.answer: Ondansetron (Zofran) is usually much less sedating, so it doesn't stack with alcohol in the same way. It isn't a green light, though: it has its own heart rhythm concerns, and blocking nausea doesn't address the cause when you've been drinking. If sedation is a problem for you, ask your prescriber whether a less sedating anti-nausea medicine makes sense.

faq.question: Is promethazine an antihistamine?
faq.answer: Yes. Promethazine is a phenothiazine-type first-generation antihistamine. Beyond blocking histamine, it also blocks dopamine, acetylcholine, and alpha-adrenergic receptors, which is why it works for nausea and why it's more sedating than many allergy pills. Like other first-generation antihistamines, it adds to alcohol's sedating effects.

faq.question: Does DHM make it safe to drink on promethazine?
faq.answer: No. There's no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation or breathing risks of combining promethazine with alcohol. DHM research is promising but early and mostly from animal studies, and little is known about how it interacts with sedating medicines. Don't use it on a night you've taken promethazine, and ask your pharmacist before combining it with any sedating prescription.
